Ungodly
un-GOD-lee
adj. and n. (without reverence toward God, impious; rendering Hebrew rasha, beliyya'al, Greek asebes)
English formation from un- and godly. It renders Greek asebes — a, without, and sebomai, to reverence: the ungodly man is not chiefly an immoral man but an irreverent one, and the immorality follows.

Biblical Definition

The ungodly are those without reverence toward God, and the Psalter opens by defining the blessed man against them in a descending sequence: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psalm 1:1). Walking, standing, sitting — the progression from passing interest to settled residence is the psalm's warning, and it begins with taking counsel, which is to say with accepting the ungodly man's account of how the world works. Jude piles the root on itself four times in one verse to describe the coming judgment: “to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him” (Jude 1:15). Paul uses the same word to state the astonishing object of the atonement: “when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6), and again in the sentence that Luther found decisive — God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). This is the doctrine of justification in its most offensive form, and Paul chose the offensive word deliberately. God does not justify the improved, the sincere, or the promising; He justifies the ungodly, on the ground of a righteousness supplied to them and not produced by them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Without reverence toward God. Psalm 1 traces the descent from walking in their counsel to sitting in the seat of the scornful; Jude hammers the root four times over the judgment; and Paul says Christ died for the ungodly and that God justifies the ungodly.

expand to see more

UNGODLY, a. Wicked; impious; neglecting the fear and worship of God, or violating his commands.

2. Polluted by wickedness, or by violation of God's law.

3. In Scripture, the class opposed to the righteous; as the counsel of the ungodly. Ps. 1.

UNGODLINESS, n. Impiety; wickedness; neglect of God and his commands.

5. Contempt of the divine character and government.

Key Scripture

Psalm 1:1 — "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful."

Romans 5:6 — "For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly."

Jude 1:15 — "To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him."

1 Timothy 1:9 — "Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,"

Modern Corruption

Ungodly has been reduced to a synonym for morally coarse — a description of other people's vices — which loses the word's actual content (irreverence toward God) and blunts the point of the verse that says Christ died for exactly such men.

expand to see more

In common religious speech ungodly now means roughly disreputable, and it is applied outward: the ungodly are the coarse, the vulgar, the obviously immoral, over there. The Greek locates it elsewhere. Asebes is the failure to reverence, and a man may be scrupulously respectable and thoroughly asebes, which is why Paul lists the ungodly alongside the profane in 1 Timothy 1:9 and why the Pharisees, not the publicans, drew Christ's hardest words. Psalm 1 makes the danger a matter of counsel before it is a matter of conduct: what the ungodly offer first is not an invitation to vice but an explanation of life that leaves God out. That is available in perfectly polite forms, and it is generally where the walking begins.

The graver loss is what happens to Romans 4:5 and 5:6 when the word is softened. Paul says God justifieth the ungodly, and the sentence is scandalous by design — it is precisely what a righteous judge must not do (Proverbs 17:15), and Paul knows it, which is why Romans 3:26 labours to show how God can be just and the justifier. The medieval system could not tolerate the sentence and read justification as the making-righteous of a man being gradually improved; the Reformation recovered it as a declaration made about the ungodly on the ground of an alien righteousness imputed. Every softening of the word softens the doctrine. If the justified are the mildly-in-need-of-help rather than the ungodly, then grace is assistance and not resurrection.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rasha (wicked, guilty) and beliyya'al (worthlessness); Greek asebes (irreverent, impious, from a + sebomai, to reverence) and asebeia (ungodliness).

expand to see more

Hebrew rasha (H7563) — wicked, guilty, condemned; the word in Psalm 1:1 rendered ungodly.

Hebrew beliyya'al (H1100) — worthlessness, ruin; rendered ungodly men in 2 Samuel 22:5 and Belial elsewhere.

Greek asebes (G765) — irreverent, impious, ungodly; the word in Romans 4:5, 5:6, and 1 Timothy 1:9.

Greek asebeia (G763) — ungodliness, impiety; the first thing named in the revelation of God's wrath in Romans 1:18.

Greek sebomai (G4576) — to revere, worship; the positive root the alpha-privative negates.

Usage

"“Walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly” — the descent begins with an account of life that leaves God out."

"“Christ died for the ungodly” — the object of the atonement stated in its most offensive terms."

"“All that are ungodly… ungodly deeds… ungodly committed… ungodly sinners” — Jude will not let the word be softened."
